evidence: The Canonical Workload box states: "Mean request service time (planning headline — not used for occupancy) ~10 s [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] — an author-chosen round planning headline. Adding ~15% headroom to 8.70 s gives 10.005 s, so the arithmetic is acceptable, but the prose says the component sum is "~8.7 s" and then says "plus ~15% planning headroom to ~10 s"—the reader must infer whether 8.7 s already includes retrieval or not. The same page earlier says Wexec = prefill + decode ≈ 8.58 s and excludes retrieval, while this row includes retrieval in the 8.7 s component sum. The two quantities are close but differently composed, and the prose does not name the discrepancy explicitly.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the Mean request service time row to separate the two bases explicitly: (1) planning headline components including retrieval = 0.12 + 1.08 + 7.5 = 8.70 s, plus 15% headroom ≈ 10.0 s; (2) execution service time Wexec used for Little's law = 1.08 + 7.5 = 8.58 s, excluding retrieval. State that 8.70 s and 8.58 s differ by the 0.12 s retrieval term, and that neither is a measured p95/p99.

chapter: Chapter 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
evidence: "At 10 rps average, the system processes ~92,000 input tokens/s + ~3,000 output tokens/s. The dollar denominator must be the whole fleet that serves this rate, not one host. At the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour (≈ $0.0333 per second), so ~92,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~2.76 million input tokens per $1 of fleet spend and ~3,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~90,000 output tokens per $1 — the active-hours basis ..."
issue: The tokens-per-dollar arithmetic divides a per-second token rate by a per-second dollar rate, which is dimensionally valid only if both rates are on the same time basis. The prose then mixes this with an active-hours monthly spend ($20,800/mo over 173.33 h) and a paid-occupancy monthly spend ($87,600/mo over 730 h). The ~2.76M and ~655K figures are later correctly identified as an hour-basis mismatch, but the initial sentence presents ~2.76M as if it were a clean per-dollar figure without naming the active-hours basis in the same sentence. The row is salvageable, but the presentation invites the exact cross-basis comparison the chapter warns against.
fix_instruction: State the active-hours basis directly in the sentence that derives ~2.76M: "on the active-hours basis, $120/hr × 173.33 h/mo ≈ $20,800/mo over 6.24M requests, giving ~2.76M input tokens per $1." Then present ~655K only as the wall-clock paid-occupancy artifact, and repeat that neither is a per-request marginal cost.

chapter: Chapter 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
evidence: "At 10 concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB of KV on top of the 140 GB weights — 381 GB of the 640 GB pool — and the pool presses well before concurrency reaches 100 (~17 full-context requests once the ~64 GB runtime is reserved: 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5, floored to 17 — the input-only 24.1 GB figure above would give 436 ÷ 24.1 ≈ 18 before the output tokens are counted). issue: The paragraph says the 17-slot ceiling is a per-host figure, then immediately says its binding limit is per-rank and gives a per-rank calculation at 17.5 slots. The 17.5-slot value is the analytical quotient before flooring; the deployed whole-slot ceiling is 17. The per-rank note uses 17.5 slots, which is the unfloored quotient, and the sentence does not reconcile 17.5 with the stated whole-slot convention (17). A reader can mistake 17.5 for a deployable slot count.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the sentence to distinguish three quantities explicitly: (1) analytical quotient C = 436 ÷ 24.9 ≈ 17.5; (2) deployable whole-context slots = floor(17.5) = 17; (3) per-rank check at the analytical quotient (17.5 slots) shows the rank is 99.97% full, so 17 whole slots is the conservative deployed ceiling. Do not use 17.5 as if it were a whole-slot count.

chapter: Chapter 5 — From Workload to Model Selection
evidence: "The ~50 tok/s here (this worked example’s low-batch decode point, ~20 ms/token — the canonical batch-1 rate at 25 ms/token is ~40 tok/s, Ch 2) and Chapter 15’s prefill-side rate are therefore different phases of the same host, not two values for one quantity.
